articles.title: How Russian dissidents are pressing for action on Putin in DC
articles.summary: Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Moscow-based journalist Dmitry Muratov is careful about what he says and for good reason. He was assaulted in 2022 with red paint laced with acetone, and he’s seen colleagues murdered or forced into exile and his newspaper shut down. In a rare appearance in Washington, D.C. on Monday, he spoke…
articles.body:
Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Moscow-based journalist Dmitry Muratov is careful about what he says and for good reason.

He was assaulted in 2022 with red paint laced with acetone, and he’s seen colleagues murdered or forced into exile and his newspaper shut down.

In a rare appearance in Washington, D.C. on Monday, he spoke about the human rights abuses Russian President Vladimir Putin’s regime is carrying out against political opponents and those critical of the war in Ukraine.

His Nobel recognition provides some protection in Putin’s Russia.

But Muratov is careful not to discuss how he continues to travel, speak abroad and carry out his journalistic work. He’s also careful not to share his opinion on global sanctions against Russia. Such remarks could see Muratov put behind bars with Russia’s approximately 1,400 to 1,700 political prisoners.

“My story is about putting the person at the center of things, at that point we can also start the process toward peace,” he told the small gathering in Washington.

The Ben Franklin Fellowship, an organization made up of current and former diplomats as well as international affairs experts who largely align with President Trump’s foreign policy, hosted the event in Washington on Monday. Muratov’s appearance comes during a flurry of activity in Washington surrounding Russia’s war in Ukraine. Congress passed legislation on Wednesday granting Trump tariff authorities against countries who purchase Russian energy.

And a major gathering of Russian dissidents and former political prisoners also took place this week. The Free Russia Foundation — founded by individuals the Kremlin has labeled extremists and terrorists — and the congressionally funded nonprofit National Endowment for Democracy hosted the “Washington Dialogue” conference in D.C.

In recognition of the Washington Dialogue, Sens. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) and Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) introduced a resolution Wednesday urging the State Department to work more closely with Russia’s opposition inside the country and in exile.

Muratov won’t be at the conference, however. Natalia Arno, president of the Free Russia Foundation, praised Muratov’s appearance in Washington and added she was careful not to approach him at the gathering. She wanted to avoid giving the Kremlin an excuse to accuse him of associating with “terrorists.”

“He’s really the most recognizable, most respected symbol of independent Russian journalism,” she said.

“Again, him still living and working inside Russia, it’s really a huge deal, and I think it also challenges Putin’s main narrative, that basically there is no opposition to him,” Arno added.

Trump has recently revived efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine as the U.S. war against Iran spirals and sends global energy prices soaring. Trump announced on Monday an effort to get both Moscow and Kyiv to halt attacks on each other’s energy facilities and stabilize oil prices.

The president’s top envoys for negotiations — his son-in-law Jared Kushner, and close friend and business partner Steve Witkoff — met Putin in Moscow earlier this month and made their first-ever visit to Kyiv to speak with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

In remarks at the Republican National Committee’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas last week, Trump said Putin was willing to come to an agreement and blamed Zelensky as the obstacle. It was a swing back by Trump toward favoring Moscow after he had signaled greater support for Ukraine.

“I understand President Trump is trying to save Putin’s face, and he thinks that Putin will be more willing to do things,” Arno said. “I think it’s wrong to try to please the dictators, the dictator will never play according to civilized norms, according to civilized rule.”

Arno said that Russian society is brewing — not yet boiling — in its agitation toward Putin and the war in Ukraine, which has stretched on for more than four years, dubbed a “special military operation” by the Kremlin. Arno said this moment is important for the U.S. to engage with Russian civil society actors that are working to survive and be ready to act for a time when Putin is gone.

Activists are lobbying the Trump administration to demand the release of political prisoners inside Russia as a necessary first step. It’s a shrewd appeal to the president, who relishes the power of freeing people wrongfully imprisoned. He often boasts of his success in freeing a Christian pastor imprisoned in Turkey as well as aiding in the return of an estimated 100 Americans unjustly detained or held hostage and the release of hundreds of more political prisons in Belarus.

In August, Trump celebrated Russia’s release of American Robert Gilman after four years in detention. But Putin has yet to release American Stephen Hubbard, among other Americans detained in Russia.

“I want to say, let Witkoff and Kushner go to Moscow as much as possible, but why are they coming back with an empty plane? Why didn’t they bring anyone back?” Muratov said at the event.

In measured remarks — and contrary to Arno’s position — Muratov called for engaging Putin’s “friends,” like right-wing parties in Europe or U.S. officials who have expressed sympathy toward Russia, suggesting that Putin might be more open to ideas about ending the war coming from voices he doesn’t consider enemies.

“I addressed the right-wing parties in the European Parliament, and in America you have people who have views that are close to Putin, they can influence the decisions Putin makes,” he said.

Muratov called for the U.S. to push for a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, an exchange of prisoners of war and political prisoners, and a guarantee that there are no strikes during the winter — a particularly cruel Russian military strategy that froze Ukrainians in their home earlier this year.

Backing that call are two Russian Orthodox priests who refused to bless the Russian invasion into Ukraine.

Father Andrei Kordochkin and Father Valerian Dunin-Barkovsky are the founders of Peace Unto All, a Russian civic group that supports Russian clergy persecuted for their opposition to the war in Ukraine. They estimate dozens of church officials are jailed in Russia or the occupied territories, from the Orthodox church and other denominations.

Kordochkin and Dunin-Barkovsky, who live outside of Russia, came to the U.S. to attend the Washington Dialogue and accept an award from the National Endowment for Democracy for promoting freedom of religion. Their mission is countering Putin’s use of the Russian Orthodox Church to bless the war in Ukraine as a “holy war.”

“What the Russian state is not going to tolerate is any personal or institutional moral authority which is autonomous from the state. This is why we are dangerous,” Kordochkin said.

The Russian opposition is far from united, and Kordochkin said that Peace Unto All does not share all the same positions. But he said it’s important to stand together against Putin’s repression.

“We think it is important to be with these people because ultimately whether they are believers or not, the values we share of human freedom, of human dignity are the same for all of us.”

articles.title: UK charities, protest groups condemn Israeli ban threat after sanctions
articles.summary: Having warned London of ‘consequences’ for sanctions, Israel targets UK charities, campaign groups and Palestine Action.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – British charities, Palestinian advocacy organisations and the proscribed Palestine Action group have condemned an official Israeli letter maligning their representatives and activists and recommending they be barred from entering Israel.

The document, seen by Al Jazeera, was issued by Israel’s Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism. It recommends border authorities bar employees and activists associated with aid organisations including Oxfam, Islamic Relief Worldwide, Save the Children, Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) and the Norwegian Refugee Council, which receives UK funding, as well as campaign groups including the Palestine Solidarity Campaign and Friends of Al-Aqsa.

The letter, dated September 8, the day the UK banned imports from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, was previously reported by the BBC and Jerusalem Post.

Ismail Patel, founder of Friends of Al-Aqsa, which openly advocates for the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement , is accused in the letter of joining anti-Israel demonstrations in London and making “harsh statements against Israel” in public appearances and interviews.

“To hear Israel is planning to ban Friends of Al-Aqsa for our BDS campaign clearly shows BDS is working and impacting Israel,” Patel told Al Jazeera. “Israeli restrictions will not intimidate us.”

Israel’s Diaspora Affairs Ministry did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

Israel follows through on threat of ‘consequences’

Israel had warned the UK against the new sanctions, with its Ministry of Foreign Affairs raising the prospect of “consequences” for what it called “hostile moves”.

Shortly after the trade ban was announced, Israel, which controls access to Gaza and the occupied West Bank, barred 11 British MPs and a lawyer from entering and ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem. It also announced the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center located in Kiryat Gat, southern Israel. And it has ended British training of Palestinian Authority forces in the occupied West Bank.

“In light of this [the trade ban], attention should be directed to the ongoing and subversive activities of various British organisations promoting boycotts, sanctions, and economic and political measures against the State of Israel,” the leaked letter reads.

It makes further accusations against 11 groups in total. The claims against them range from advocating for engagement with Hamas for humanitarian access; demanding an arms embargo against Israel; having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood or working with “terrorist” organisations.

Save the Children is accused of describing Israel’s actions as “deliberate starvation” and “genocide”.

A spokesperson told Al Jazeera that, alongside other NGOs, it is already unable to secure visas for staff needing to cross Israeli-controlled borders into Gaza or the West Bank, “at a time when needs have never been greater”.

Israel has intensified restrictions on international aid groups since the genocidal war in Gaza began, including measures affecting the entry of food , medicine, foreign volunteer doctors and humanitarian workers.

MAP said the letter forms part of Israeli authorities’ “wider restrictions on international charities operating in the occupied Palestinian territory”. It noted that two MAP individuals named in the letter had received the humanitarian medals awarded by King Charles.

The letter describes Palestine Action , which has carried out raids against Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems, as a “network of radical branches promoting direct action intended to damage the Israeli defence industry”.

“This letter is further proof that we were not banned because of anything to do with ‘terrorism’,” Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori told Al Jazeera. “As the letter admits, our activity was always focused on damaging the Israeli defence industry.”

In a related development, UK Lawyers for Israel has called on the government to consider proscribing Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, as a terrorist organisation, The Telegraph reported. The lobby group alleged, in line with Israeli accusations, that MSF had employed people with links to Palestinian armed groups.

MSF said it had been the target of a “disinformation campaign” for months. It said staff accused by Israel of having “ties to terrorism” were only reported to the organisation after they had been killed, and that Israeli authorities had not shared evidence of military involvement before their deaths.

articles.title: Lebanon security talks in Paris to focus on post-UNIFIL alternatives
articles.summary: The security talks come as Israeli forces continue attacks across southern Lebanon despite a “ceasefire”.
articles.body:
European and Arab military chiefs are meeting in Paris to assess the Lebanese Armed Forces’ needs and discuss the looming end of the United Nations peacekeeping mission UNIFIL, amid fears of a renewed Israeli military campaign in southern Lebanon.

Thursday’s talks will initially be chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron alongside Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Jordan’s King Abdullah II.

The United States will be represented by a senior military official involved in Middle East security issues, the Reuters news agency reported.

The meetings come after Israel and Lebanon held ⁠several rounds of US-brokered talks aimed at easing tensions along their border.

A US-mediated framework deal was agreed between Israel and Lebanon in June, but the agreement did not force Israel to withdraw from the large area of southern Lebanon it occupies, and Israel has continued its attacks on the country.

On Wednesday night, Israeli forces carried out a series of attacks across southern Lebanon, according to the country’s National News Agency.

Meanwhile, Israeli air attacks killed at least 13 people , including six children, in a town in southern Lebanon last week, according to Lebanon’s Ministry of Public Health, in one of the deadliest days of Israeli bombardment in ‌recent weeks.

The most immediate concern of the meeting in Paris will be the security vacuum that could be ⁠left when the almost 50-year mission of UNIFIL, which has about 7,500 personnel, ⁠leaves in January.

Despite Lebanon and France both favouring an extension of the UN mandate, neither the US nor Israel has signalled support for prolonging the mission.

The officials in Paris will discuss options for a new international mission, backed by France and Italy, operating outside a ⁠UN mandate, as well as a possible European Union-led mission.

Both concepts would reportedly focus on training, equipment, intelligence sharing, and mentoring support for the Lebanese Armed Forces.

Paris said it wanted the “operational context, parameters and modalities” of the deployment to be clarified at Thursday’s discussions, as a prerequisite for what it hopes will be “robust” international support for the Lebanese forces.

Fears of a renewed Israeli military campaign are growing in Lebanon after escalating attacks, despite a “ceasefire” that was intended to halt Israeli aggression and allow the thousands of displaced people in Lebanon to return home.

Disarming the Lebanese armed group Hezbollah remains a key condition for Israel’s withdrawal from southern Lebanon, according to the deal signed, with Aoun reiterating his determination to disarm the group, but “without confrontation”.

articles.title: AI bosses say they can self-regulate and House passes Russia sanctions bill: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: AI executives call for self-regulation of their companies’ technology.
articles.body: AI executives call for self-regulation of their companies’ technology. Trump reacts to the Fed’s decision to hike interest rates. And the L.A. news community mourns those killed in a helicopter crash. Here’s what to know today. AI giants call for creating their own rules Concerns about artificial intelligence and the pace of its development have exploded in recent days. Now, tech executives — including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Open AI CEO Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis — are coalescing around the idea that their industry needs to come up with its own rules and standards. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Tech companies have shown some willingness to make changes — but without regulation, they’re also able to undo those changes whenever they want. Litigation has also moved companies to change, like Meta’s recent $18 billion settlement, which included an agreement to place limits on how teens use Instagram. But some experts question AI companies’ ability to regulate themselves. “Self regulation is an oxymoron,” said Alex Bores, a New York state assemblyman and supporter of nationwide AI regulation. “That’s just Congress and the president not living up to their duty to protect the American people.” The House yesterday overwhelmingly passed a bill that would shield consumers from higher energy costs from new data centers in their communities. But the bill doesn’t address recent safety concerns, and it’s uncertain what will happen to the bill in the Senate. Meanwhile, people across the political spectrum, from Steve Bannon to Sen. Bernie Sanders, have called for a “pro-human” future for AI (more on that in today’s Staff Pick). Where things stand with AI self-regulation. More AI coverage: As industry worries swell over the technology’s rapid progress, OpenAI disclosed six new incidents of “unexpected or concerning” behavior by its artificial intelligence models. The company also unveiled a new framework for tracking and reporting these instances of what it termed “misalignment.” An NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey found that 53% of adults believe AI does more harm than good in K-12 education, and 54% believe the same in colleges and universities. Fed raises interest rates for the first time since 2023 The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in three years and signaled one more interest rate hike in the coming months as it aims to slow rising inflation. The central bank raised rates yesterday 0.25%, making its flagship rate 4.00%. And as of this week, all but two members of the Federal Open Market Committee forecast another rate increase this year. Inflation was up to 3.4% as of August, fueled by the Iran war’s impact on energy prices. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters that his agency can’t affect the prices of food and other items, “but what we can do, and will do, is ensure that any change in relative prices don’t broaden out.” President Donald Trump reacted to the decision by demanding interest rates be lowered, “AND FAST!” He later said the Fed’s decision was due to a “hostile board” that Warsh couldn’t overpower. “I told, I talked to Kevin, and I think if you want to approach the board, it’s not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They’re very political. They’re doing the wrong thing.” Trump also rejected the claim that rates were raised to combat inflation, arguing the board was “raising them only for political reasons.” What Warsh said about the Fed’s decision. House passes Russia sanctions bill and leaves Washington A bill aimed at imposing sanctions on Russia and Iran is headed to President Donald Trump’s desk for his signature after it passed in the House yesterday in a 262-159 vote. The legislation, named the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, takes aim at Russia’s energy sector by punishing the largest buyers of its oil and gas, allowing the president to impose tariffs on goods from those countries, which may include China and India. The goal is to slash the revenue streams that fund Russia’s ongoing war on Ukraine. But some top House Democrats who criticized the bill fear it would grant broad tariff authorities that Trump could abuse. Here’s what else the bill states. After voting wrapped yesterday, House members left Washington and aren’t expected to reconvene until Nov. 9 — after the midterm elections. That means lawmakers won’t vote on Rep. Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which needs to be acted on in two legislative days. While GOP leaders insisted their decision to cancel today’s votes had nothing to do with Massie’s impeachment efforts, it allowed vulnerable Republican members to avoid a difficult vote on Hegseth’s leadership during the unpopular six-month war with Iran. What Speaker Mike Johnson said of Massie’s impeachment effort. Separately, human rights experts commissioned by the U.N.’s top human rights body say they have found “reasonable grounds” to believe the U.S. committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran, including on a school in the southern city of Minab. More politics news: For subscribers: Election officials are caught in the middle of the fight in Missouri over which congressional map will be in place for the midterm elections. “Somebody I talked to … described it as being the ping-pong ball in a ping-pong game,” one official said. For subscribers: The Democratic Party’s left flank has a chance to win big in battleground races. Michigan is at the center of the fight. Helicopter crash shatters a tight-knit local news community Los Angeles’ TV news community was in mourning the day after a helicopter used by the local NBC station crashed while covering a fatal bus collision, killing three people. Journalist Eliana Moreno, 38, was remembered as dependable and kind to her colleagues. Pilot George Marciniw was praised for his professionalism and devotion to his job. Edy Fernando Gutiérrez Mejia, 29, a pedestrian who died at the scene, was affectionately known as “Pichi” to loved ones. Learn more about the victims. Tuesday’s crash played out in on-air remarks and in social media posts as anchors and reporters processed their grief while continuing to report on the accident. Colleen Williams, a 40-year veteran of NBC Los Angeles and one of the city’s most recognizable broadcasting personalities, seemed to fight back tears as she confirmed on air that the station’s helicopter had gone down. Robert Kovacik, a 22-year veteran of the station, wiped away tears from inside a police vehicle. The heartbreak extended to other news stations. “What happens in this business is you wind up spending holidays, weekends, late nights and early mornings with these people, your colleagues,” said Jeff Wald, former news director at local station KTLA. “They become your second family.” How the L.A. news community mourned its own. Staff Pick: Inside the ‘Pro-Human’ AI summit For years, I’ve chatted and met with people skeptical of the speed of AI development — some of them award-winning physicists who worry that a super intelligence could supplant human ingenuity, others activists who have railed against the growing concentration of wealth and power for a select few tech oligarchs. Those factions, and more, convened for the first Pro-Human Assembly in Washington, D.C., this week. Faith leaders, A(ish)- list actors, computer scientists, nonprofit activists and more advocated for a more human approach to AI development. The conference had an incredible buzz, especially coming off the heels of last week’s firestorm of headlines about how AI researchers think the technology is moving too fast. There was also a table of free merchandise — I don’t know the next time I’ll be able to nab a free baseball hat that proclaims the benefits of being “pro-human.” Despite the camaraderie, attendees seemed to disagree on what “pro-human” actually meant. Steve Bannon railed against China, while Sen. Bernie Sanders advocated for people to have a democratic say in the technology’s direction. articles.body: El liderazgo diario de MARCA.com en la prensa española sigue siendo incontestable e indiscutible. Nuestro sitio web es el más leído de España día tras día tanto en los medios deportivos como generalistas, según el informe correspondiente al mes de agosto elaborado por GfK, el medidor oficial de audiencias digitales del país, que sitúa a MARCA al frente en todas las métricas de calidad. articles.title: Massie: GOP leaders found ‘other Republicans’ who would join Hegseth impeachment push
articles.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) argued Wednesday that House GOP leaders sent the lower chamber home early because they found other Republicans in support of his push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. “The fact that they didn’t vote on it tells me that they did a whip check, and they probably found that there were…
articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) argued Wednesday that House GOP leaders sent the lower chamber home early because they found other Republicans in support of his push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“The fact that they didn’t vote on it tells me that they did a whip check, and they probably found that there were some other Republicans, besides me, that were going to vote for this, or at least didn’t wanna be on the record supporting Hegseth,” he told host Kaitlan Collins on CNN’s “The Source.”

The outgoing Kentucky libertarian, a frequent critic of President Trump, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Tuesday.

Massie accused Hegseth of violating his “oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States,” citing his handling of the Iran war and operations to kill alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean.

The GOP lawmaker, who lost his primary in May to Trump-backed Ed Gallrein, also made his impeachment resolution privileged.

That would have forced lawmakers to vote on it within two days, before Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) sent them home a day early for a seven-week recess.

Given that, Massie argued the early recess was because of his impeachment resolution.

“I know it was,” he told Collins, adding it is “actually bad politics” to have the resolution “hanging over Pete Hegseth’s head” until the House returns in November.

“If there was any other reason that they canceled tomorrow’s day of session, they could have had the Hegseth vote tonight,” the GOP lawmaker added. “Because the rules say that he has to have the vote within 48 hours. They don’t … say he has to wait 48 hours.

“So, [Johnson] could have had the vote yesterday, as soon as I introduced the articles. He could have done it today, before he adjourned Congress,” he added, later dubbing the early recess the “Hegseth holiday.”

articles.title: BRICS is challenging the US-led order but can’t replace it yet
articles.summary: The nations flocking to join BRICS want multiple centers of economic and diplomatic influence rather than reliance on a single superpower.
articles.body:
One of the biggest geopolitical stories of the 21st century is the emergence of a broad coalition of countries determined to dilute the West’s monopoly on global governance.

That coalition is informally known as BRICS , an acronym that stands for the grouping’s five original members: Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. Originally coined “BRIC” as a term for an international investment category, the actual nations of BRICS held their first summit using the modified name in 2011.

Since 2024, BRICS has expanded into an 11-member grouping that includes states as diverse as Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, Ethiopia and Iran.

To many Americans, BRICS is little more than an anti-Western talking shop . But it is a mistake to dismiss a coalition that represents nearly half of humanity (the Group of Seven accounts for less than 10 percent ), a growing share of global output, and an increasingly influential voice of the Global South. Whereas the G7 share of the world economy has steadily declined since the 1990s, BRICS’s share continues to rise.

Its growing influence reflects a profound reality: much of the non-Western world wants greater strategic autonomy and deeper economic cooperation beyond Western-led frameworks.

So the real question is not whether BRICS matters, but whether it can catalyze the development of a genuine alternative to the current U.S.-led world order. Its summit in New Delhi last weekend offered an illuminating answer.

The summit concluded with a 140-point New Delhi Declaration . Despite deep divisions, India brokered consensus among rivals by grounding the text in established U.N. legal frameworks and other standard multilateral principles.

But the summit also underscored a central paradox: BRICS members agree that the international system is unfair because it does not reflect today’s distribution of economic and political power. Yet they disagree deeply about what should replace it — or even how to begin overhauling it.

India and Brazil advocate reforming institutions such as the U.N. Security Council, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank to give developing countries greater representation. They want to keep BRICS as non-Western but not to let it become anti-Western.

China and Russia, in contrast, are often more interested in building parallel structures to curtail Western influence altogether.

And then some newer members, such as Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Egypt, maintain close security ties with the U.S., even as they deepen engagement with BRICS. The Emiratis and Saudis even host American military bases. Being part of BRICS allows these countries to diversify their geopolitical options and build alternative partnerships to help insulate themselves from Washington’s policy swings.

BRICS’s initiatives include local currency settlements, alternative payment mechanisms, and development financing through its New Development Bank . They are designed not so much to directly challenge the dollar’s global dominance — which in any case is eroding — as to reduce vulnerability to unilateral Western sanctions. BRICS essentially functions as a geopolitical hedge.

From Washington’s perspective, BRICS is best understood not as an anti-American alliance but as a coalition of countries seeking to reduce dependence on U.S.-led institutions. For many member states, BRICS is largely about expanding their diplomatic and economic choices.

Yet the New Delhi Declaration also exposed one of BRICS’s major weaknesses: its own double standards.

The declaration strongly condemns “unilateral coercive measures,” language aimed primarily at U.S. sanctions and trade levies such as the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. That criticism resonates across much of the non-Western world, where many governments view such unilateral action as something the Western-dominated international system makes possible.

But the declaration had one conspicuous omission: China is increasingly employing export restrictions on rare earths, critical minerals, manufacturing equipment and key industrial components as instruments of geopolitical leverage, including against its own BRICS partners.

For example, Beijing has recently imposed formal and informal India-specific export curbs , which have been widely interpreted as efforts to slow India’s emergence as an alternative global manufacturing hub. If unilateral economic coercion is objectionable when practiced by Washington, how can it be ignored when practiced by Beijing?

The answer has much to do with the mechanics of consensus diplomacy. Every BRICS declaration requires unanimous approval. So members are willing to collectively criticize external powers, but they have little space to name coercive behavior within their own ranks.

That, in turn, reveals an uncomfortable truth: BRICS is often united more by what it opposes than by what it practices — or by any shared vision of the alternative international order it hopes to build.

None of this means the U.S. should underestimate the organization. BRICS has already succeeded in signaling that the era of Western dominance is drawing to a close. More than three dozen countries have formally applied or expressed interest in joining BRICS, including states that remain close U.S. allies, such as Bahrain and Turkey, a NATO member.

The attraction is that BRICS helps broaden international options for governments, many of which increasingly want multiple centers of economic and diplomatic influence rather than reliance on a single superpower.

For Washington, ignoring legitimate demands for greater representation in global institutions would be counterproductive to its own interest in upholding the present international order. A willingness to reform multilateral governance may prove more effective than attempting to preserve structures designed in and for 1945.

The New Delhi summit may have demonstrated both the promise and the limits of BRICS. It is an influential coalition but not yet a unified alliance. It can coordinate diplomatic messaging but struggles to reconcile rival national ambitions. Its members share strong dissatisfaction with the current order but remain divided over the architecture of the next.

Such underlying strain does not diminish BRICS’s significance. The future order will likely be shaped by a diverse group of middle powers seeking a multipolar world in which no single nation or bloc writes all the rules, East or West.

Brahma Chellaney is the author of nine books, including the award-winning “Water: Asia’s New Battleground .”

articles.title: Faint signal leads treasure hunters to massive discovery at legendary 400-year-old wreck
articles.summary: A 55-pound copper ingot worth up to $25,000 was pulled from the Atocha shipwreck site in the Florida Keys. The treasure-hunting crew says more great finds await.
articles.body: A treasure-hunting crew searching a legendary 17th-century underwater shipwreck off the Florida Keys has recovered a massive 55-pound copper ingot — the latest find along a trail that its captain believes could lead to more treasure. The ingot was found by divers with Mel Fisher's Shipwreck Expeditions at the wreck site of the Nuestra Señora de Atocha, about 35 miles west of Key West. The Spanish treasure galleon was on its return voyage to Spain when it sank in a hurricane off the Florida Keys in 1622 — carrying silver, gold and emeralds. MYSTERY OF GOLD COIN SHIPWRECK FINALLY UNMASKED AFTER 30 YEARS: 'FANTASTIC CONCLUSION' Mel Fisher began searching for the Atocha in 1969. He spent years recovering artifacts from the wreck before his company prevailed in a lengthy legal battle over rights to its treasure in 1982. Fisher's team discovered the Atocha's famed "Mother Lode," or main cargo deposit, in 1985 — and the site still yields new finds decades later. Photos show the 55-pound copper ingot — or copper bar — heavily coated in marine encrustation after spending over four centuries underwater. In an August press release, Mel Fisher's Shipwreck Expeditions said the ingot has an estimated value of about $18,000 to $25,000. UNDERWATER ROBOTICS EXPERT REVEALS 'SHIPWRECK CITY' HIDING BENEATH MAJOR URBAN LAKE Captain Drake Nicholas was retracing an area from the salvage vessel DARE when his metal detector picked up a faint signal, he told Fox News Digital. The captain said he was following a "tight trail of coins" at the time. "I thought it was a cannon, but it ended up being a copper ingot, which was also very exciting." "Faint hits are always the most exciting because they lead to, you know, stuff very deep in the mud," said Nicholas. "And I got that very faint hit. I dug down like I always do ... and it got louder, and that's, you know, when the excitement really kicks in." DIVERS UNCOVER HUNDREDS OF ANCIENT RELICS NEAR SHIPWRECK UNTOUCHED FOR 2,100 YEARS Nicholas said he initially mistook the ingot for a cannon due to its rounded shape, large size and bronze-copper coloring. "I was so excited," he said. "I thought it was a cannon, but it ended up being a copper ingot, which was also very exciting." Though the ingot may appear ordinary to the untrained eye, Nicholas said copper was a "very precious" resource in the 1600s — especially for making the bronze cannons that the Spanish Empire relied on. MAN FISHING WITH GRANDSON UNCOVERS MYSTERY WRECKAGE IN MUD FLATS, ARCHAEOLOGISTS INVESTIGATING "I believe that only certain people could actually own copper because it was making such strong cannons," he said. "It wasn't something [that] an everyday guy could have a stockpile of — it was more for the king and queen to make cannons." To make the ingots, metalworkers "would basically dig a hole in the sand and just pour copper into it," he said. "It would make this copper ingot or a copper bar," added Nicholas. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "They were very crude, not many markings on them, a lot of impurities in them, but it was copper being sent over to Spain for bronze cannons." The recent discoveries have given Nicholas reason to believe the crew may be closing in on a larger concentration of treasure. "The size of what we've been finding lately is … leading us to what I believe is the rest of the treasure," Nicholas said. Part of that confidence comes from new technology that Nicholas said allows the crew to detect targets deeper beneath the dense mud covering the site. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "We've never really [gotten] to penetrate that mud with a metal detector to get down and find, you know, the rest of the silver bars, copper ingots and coins," he said. "Right now, I have 19 targets that are very interesting, very high-value targets that I'm going out after next," added Nicholas. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "And it's a lot of digging through that mud and getting down to that level. But once I'm there, I'm very, very confident and excited — we're just very excited to see where this is leading." The latest discovery follows another recent find from the Atocha shipwreck. articles.title: Trump: EU allowing Canada to become associate member could be ‘hostile act’
articles.summary: President Trump said Wednesday the European Union (EU) inviting Canada to join as an associate member could amount to a “hostile act,” threatening tariffs or a trade embargo against the bloc. “If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe,”…
articles.body:
President Trump said Wednesday the European Union (EU) inviting Canada to join as an associate member could amount to a “hostile act,” threatening tariffs or a trade embargo against the bloc.

“If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe,” Trump told reporters in North Carolina, while stumping for GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley on the campaign trail.

The president called the idea of Canada joining the EU “laughable,” and blasted the U.S.’s northern neighbor as a “terrible trade partner” amid his tariff war with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine,” Trump noted. “If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday she wants Canada to join the EU as its first-ever associate member.

“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union,” von der Leyen remarked at her annual State of the Union address in France , with Carney in attendance.

During remarks to the European Parliament on Thursday, Carney called for “deep cooperation” between his country and the EU on issues such as critical minerals, defense industrial capacity and artificial intelligence.

“Deepening and widening our relationship will strengthen our sovereignty, improve affordability, opportunity, and security for our citizens, while safeguarding our ability to live our lives as we choose,” the prime minister said.

Carney later remarked, “We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

Trump and Carney have exchanged tariffs on goods imported between the two countries in recent weeks, with Ottawa matching the U.S. president’s 50 percent levies on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods.

The standoff will impact U.S. industries, such as steel and aluminum, and has thrown a wrench into the relationship with America’s second-largest trading partner.

Carney did not name Trump in his Thursday address, but he said earlier this month that he is ushering in a new era for Canada — one which is not defined by “dependence” on the U.S.

“The past 40 years has been a period of deeper economic integration with the United States. Truth is, it was easy business, but it meant we relied too much on one economic partner,” he said in a video his office posted to YouTube. “It’s clear that time is over.”

articles.title: Father of Noah Woods pays tribute to 'sweetest little boy'
articles.summary: Rhys Woods pays tribute to his three-year-old son and offers "deepest gratitude" for community support.
articles.body:
The father of Noah Woods has said the three-year-old "will be loved forever" and no words can describe the pain of the family's loss.

Noah disappeared from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday after becoming separated from a relative.

At least 1,300 people helped to try to find him in the following 24 hours, before a child's body was discovered on Wednesday afternoon at a nearby pond.

"Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much," his father Rhys Woods wrote in a post on Facebook.

"This was the most heartbreaking outcome for us, we were just hoping that he would be hiding somewhere obvious where someone could find him, that's what we kept telling ourselves the whole time."

People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help with the search for Noah, who was from East Bergholt.

Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border.

Reflecting on the community response, Woods said: "It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation, you have all taken Noah into you're own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound."

He thanked everyone who came together to search for "our boy" - listing emergency services, businesses and venues in the village - and "all of the people who gave up their time in their busy schedules to help us when we most needed it".

"The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives," the post added.

"With our love and deepest gratitude, from his daddy and mummy and little brother."

He finished the post by addressing his son.

"Noah, you will be loved forever, you will never be forgotten and we miss you so so much.

"It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us."

articles.title: Carney: Canada welcomes proposal to become EU associate member
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday welcomed Canada’s invitation to join the European Union as its first associate member. “A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies,” Carney said during his speech before the European Parliament. “An alliance not defined by what we oppose but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity,…
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday welcomed Canada’s invitation to join the European Union as its first associate member.

“A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies,” Carney said during his speech before the European Parliament. “An alliance not defined by what we oppose but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability.”

The prime minister thanked European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who floated the idea a day earlier, writing on social media that it would “create a common prosperity and economic security space.”

“Canada welcomes this ambition,” he told the legislative body, noting support from Canadians in polling for “much closer ties with Europe.”

“An alliance for the future is a unique positive approach that we will define together, building on our common strengths and based on our shared values,” Carney added.

The Canadian leader proposed “deep cooperation” on issues like critical minerals, defense industrial capacity, AI, space, research and financial services.

President Trump, whose administration levied high tariffs on Canadian goods in recent weeks as trade talks fizzled , threatened more economic actions and a potential trade embargo if Canada joins the EU.

“I think it’s laughable. Canada’s been a terrible trading partner,” the president told reporters in North Carolina during a campaign rally for GOP Senate hopeful Michael Whatley. “If they do that, if I think at all it’s a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe.”

Carney received a standing ovation at the end of his Thursday remarks, in which he expressed Canada’s dedication to the blocs shared values.

“We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals,” he said.

“Our commitment to the rule of law and our unyielding defense of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication,” the prime minister continued. “We hold common values, for which we have always fought and for whose defense we must always remain vigilant.”

articles.title: Sweden prime minister to resign as left-wing bloc seals narrow election win
articles.summary: ⁠Sweden’s ⁠centre-right Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said he will resign after losing the parliamentary elections.
articles.body:
Sweden’s prime minister says he will resign after the left-wing opposition secured a narrow victory in the country’s general election, though it faces tough negotiations ahead to form a coalition government.

The vote count ended on Thursday with the Swedish Election Authority announcing that the four left-wing opposition parties won 176 seats in the 349-seat parliament in Stockholm, the Riksdag.

The four parties that make up or support the outgoing conservative-led government took 173 seats, meaning that the left-wing bloc won with a slim three-seat majority .

Only about 50,000 votes separated the two sides in the country of 10.6 million people.

Shortly after the results were announced, ⁠Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said he would resign.

“Now, ‌it is the speaker who will lead the next stage of the way to a new government. I am henceforth requesting that I be relieved of the office of prime minister to allow that ⁠work to start immediately,” Kristersson ⁠said in a letter posted on social media X.

Former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson’s centre-left Social Democrats finished as the biggest single party , despite losing some support.

The result bolsters her hope of regaining the job she lost in 2022, but she will still face a complicated task to turn it into a government due to ideological divisions within the left-leaning bloc, which is made up of the Social Democrats, the Left Party, the Greens Party and the Centre Party.

Andersson, who was Sweden’s first female prime minister in 2021-2022 and was finance minister for seven years before that, will notably need to reconcile differences between the socialist Left Party and the liberal Centre Party.

The Centre Party has said it will oppose a government that includes cabinet posts for the Left Party, which has insisted on having a minister. Andersson has meanwhile ruled out a government that includes the Left Party, but wants their support in Sweden’s parliament.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who leads one of the few left-wing governments in Europe, hailed the result.

“Social democracy has won the elections in Sweden. After four years of a right-wing government with the far right, the Swedes are once again backing the welfare state, social justice and the green agenda,” Sanchez said in a post to X.

Parliament can vote on a new prime minister on September 29 at the earliest.

Kristersson said on election night that he would respect Andersson’s attempts to form a government, but wished her “good luck” given the divisions among her left-wing bloc.

Meanwhile, in a big surprise, the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, which entered parliament in 2010, lost support for the first time , garnering 17.5 percent of the vote, down three percentage points from the last election in 2022.
